summary: This informational RFC lists requirements for a tunnel-based EAP method. The method would use TLS to set up a secure tunnel that supports password authentication, EAP authentication, and the transport of additional data.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6678 describes what a new authentication method must be able to do. The idea is to build a protected tunnel first, using the same encryption layer that secures web connections, and then run the actual password or token check inside that tunnel. The document lists the situations the method must handle and the guarantees it must give, so that a candidate method can be judged against a fixed set of requirements.

subtitle: What a protected EAP tunnel method must do before it can carry passwords, tokens and inner authentication methods.

tldr.problem: EAP has many authentication methods, some of them weak, and a weak method running on the open network can be attacked or relayed.
tldr.mechanism: A tunnel method first builds a protected tunnel with TLS and then runs the real authentication inside it. The RFC lists what such a method must support: strong cipher suites, cleartext passwords carried safely inside the tunnel, protected negotiation of the inner method, and cryptographic binding between the tunnel and the inner method.
tldr.outcome: The document is a requirements list, not a protocol. It sets the bar for the EAP method update process in the IETF, which is where a method such as EAP-TEAP was later chosen.

today: RFC 6678 is an Informational RFC published in July 2012, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sets requirements for a tunnel method rather than defining one, and it was written for the IETF method update process, where a candidate method is judged against requirements of this kind.

sections.title: An Authentication Method Inside a Protected Tunnel
sections.content:
An EAP tunnel method is an Extensible Authentication Protocol method that first establishes a secure tunnel and then executes other EAP methods under the protection of that tunnel. It can be used in any lower-layer protocol that supports EAP authentication. Several such methods already exist and all of them use Transport Layer Security (TLS) to build the tunnel, among them Protected EAP (PEAP), EAP-TTLS in RFC 5281 and EAP-FAST in RFC 4851.

This arrangement has worked well, so the RFC starts from a consensus that TLS is the right basis for another such method. The reasons for protecting an EAP exchange this way are that it shields weak authentication exchanges such as a username and password, that it can protect the peer's identity and allow several EAP methods to be chained, and that it gives a place to carry extra data for other purposes.

The document states requirements only and defines no protocol. Where it writes MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT and MAY in capitals it is using the special meanings set out in its conventions section: an absolute requirement, an absolute prohibition, a strong recommendation, a strong recommendation against, and a willingness to allow an optional outcome.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC asks for a way of putting a protected tube around an authentication exchange. TLS, the encryption layer used for secure web connections, runs the tube, and the actual password or token check happens inside it. The document lists what such a method must be able to do; it does not build one.

sections.title: Nine Situations the Method Has to Serve
sections.content:
The RFC lists nine use cases, and a candidate tunnel method must support every one of them that is marked as mandatory. Password authentication comes first. Many legacy systems need the actual username and password sent to the authentication server, so the method must carry cleartext credentials inside the tunnel without revealing anything about them to parties on the path, and it must protect against a man-in-the-middle. It must also protect weak EAP methods: EAP-MD5, for instance, gives neither mutual authentication nor protection against dictionary attacks, and running such a method inside a protected tunnel removes much of that weakness.

The other cases widen the scope. Chained EAP methods let a user and the device they are using be authenticated together, with protection against an attacker who tries to make two separate conversations look like one. Identity protection keeps the peer's identity from anyone except the server that ends the tunnel. Anonymous service access lets a user reach limited services while still deriving keys that can protect the link layer.

Network endpoint assessment, which checks the health of a device joining a network, should be carried inside the tunnel. The method must be able to authenticate the client while the tunnel is being established, must be extensible so that later authentication and access data can travel inside it, and may support authentication with no certificates at all, where the peer and the server authenticate each other with a shared password and pass credentials for later use through the tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists nine situations the new method has to handle, from sending a plain password through the protected tube to checking a device's health before letting it in. Some of these are mandatory and some are only recommended.

sections.title: What the Protected Tunnel Must Provide
sections.content:
The tunnel must be built with TLS version 1.2 as defined in RFC 5246; earlier versions above SSL 2.0 may be supported for backward compatibility. The cipher suite negotiation must be integrity protected, because an unprotected negotiation is open to a downgrade attack in which an attacker forces the two ends to agree on a weaker suite. At least one suite that every implementation must support has to give the equivalent security of 128-bit AES for encryption and message authentication. The mandatory suites must provide certificate-based authentication of the server, may provide certificate-based authentication of the client, and must not include mutually anonymous suites or static Diffie-Hellman suites.

Replay protection must come from a time-varying input such as a timestamp, a sequence number or a nonce. The method must support TLS session resumption, must be able to fragment and reassemble data that does not fit in a single EAP message, and must protect the protocol version and type code that travel outside the tunnel. The tunnel must not be tied to one cryptographic algorithm: it has to negotiate at run time among an extensible set, so that users can move off an algorithm once a weakness is found.

Inside the tunnel, the payload must be extensible, must support the request and response pattern that EAP normally uses, must let a sender mark an attribute so that the receiver reports back if it did not understand it, and must carry vendor-specific attributes in separate namespaces. It must also carry a result indication and its acknowledgement, separately for intermediate and final results, so that both ends finish in the same state, and it may support international strings encoded in UTF-8.
sections.plainLanguage: The protected tube must use TLS 1.2 or later, must protect the agreement on which encryption to use so nobody can force a weaker one, and must offer at least one strong option that every implementation has to support. Data too big for one message must be split and put back together.

sections.title: Carrying Usernames and Passwords
sections.content:
Many systems authenticate against a legacy password database or verifier, such as an LDAP directory or a one-time password system, and these need the password in its original text form. The rules the RFC sets are strict. The cleartext password exchange must be protected for both confidentiality and integrity, which is met by running it inside an authenticated and encrypted tunnel, and the server must be authenticated before the peer sends the cleartext password at all.

There is a practical wrinkle. The peer may have to send its password before it has network access, so it may not be able to check whether the server's certificate has been revoked. The method must therefore support some way of checking the revocation status of a credential, and it should use the Online Certificate Status Protocol or the Server-based Certificate Validation Protocol to obtain the revocation status of the EAP server certificate.

Usernames and passwords must also work in international languages. The method must encode them in UTF-8 and must state how usernames and passwords are normalised and compared, referring to SASLprep or Net-UTF-8 for that purpose. The exchange should carry metadata saying whether the authentication is for a user or for a machine, which matters when both are authenticated in one session, and it must support changing a password.
sections.plainLanguage: Some systems only store a password in a form the server must see in full, so the password has to be sent. The RFC says this is only allowed inside the protected tube, and only after the server has proved who it is. The exchange also has to handle passwords written in other languages.

sections.title: Binding the Tunnel to the Inner Method
sections.content:
The tunnel must carry inner EAP methods without modifying them, and must not redefine them. The negotiation of which inner method to use must itself be protected, so that an intermediary cannot manipulate it. Chaining several inner methods is recommended, and the method must be able to report intermediate results and verify the binding between the chained methods.

The most important requirement is cryptographic binding: a mechanism that ties the tunnel to the inner method. Without it an attacker can impersonate the peer to the server by relaying the inner exchange to a peer that is running the method outside a tunnel. The binding is normally made by mixing the tunnel key with the key material the inner method produced. When n inner methods run one after another, a compound key is computed after each one, so that CTK_i = f(CTK_i-1, MK_i), with CTK_0 = TK. The final compound key CTK_n then derives the EAP Master Session Key, the Extended Master Session Key and the transient encryption and integrity keys.

The RFC also requires that every derived key has a lifetime no longer than the lifetime of any key above it in the hierarchy, and that the derivation stops a compromise in one part of the system from leading to compromises in other parts that rely on keys at the same or a higher level.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel must prove that the authentication happening inside it really is talking to the same endpoints, and not to a relay. It does this by mixing the tunnel's secret key with the key the inner method produced, so a captured exchange cannot be replayed into a different tunnel.

sections.title: Where the Weaknesses Are
sections.content:
The choice of cipher suite is the first security concern. A suite with weak or no authentication, such as an anonymous Diffie-Hellman suite, greatly increases the risk that the system is compromised, and a weak encryption or integrity algorithm inside the tunnel makes the method vulnerable as well. A tunnel that supports a key establishment algorithm an adversary can break on line is open to a downgrade attack, in which the adversary breaks the weak algorithm and steps the negotiation down without being detected. A mutually anonymous tunnel is open to a man-in-the-middle who establishes one tunnel with the peer and another with the server, then reads everything inside both, including the identifiers exchanged by the EAP method.

On tunneled authentication, cryptographic binding between the inner method and the tunnel is what proves that the tunnel endpoints and the inner method share the same endpoints, and this thwarts the attack when the inner keys are strong enough not to be broken in real time. Where the inner method produces no key material, or only weak key material, security policies must forbid the peer from running that method outside a protective tunnel or against an untrustworthy server.

Two further points concern what lies outside the tunnel and where it ends. Data outside the tunnel, such as the EAP type code and version numbers, must be protected against modification. And terminating the inner method somewhere other than where the tunnel ends needs care, because the inner data can then be modified or read on the way, for example when a cleartext password travels in a RADIUS password attribute, which uses weak encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: The security section warns about weak choices of encryption suite, about an attacker who forces both ends onto a weaker one, and about a man in the middle who sits between the peer and the server. It also warns that ending the tunnel in one place and the authentication in another can expose the password.

viz.caption: WHAT THE TUNNEL PAYLOAD MUST CARRY

items.title: Extensible attributes
items.text: New data types can be added to the payload later.

items.title: Request and response
items.text: The half-duplex pattern that EAP normally uses.

items.title: Criticality marking
items.text: A sender can ask to be told if an attribute was not understood.

items.title: Vendor namespaces
items.text: Vendor-specific attributes are kept in separate, named spaces.

items.title: Result indication
items.text: Intermediate and final results are reported separately and acknowledged.
